summary: This document fixes weaknesses in OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication when keys are managed manually. The existing mechanism is vulnerable to replay attacks within and across sessions, and this extension adds protections against them.

eli5.summary: Without care, a bad person could record a valid message and play it back later. This adds a way to tell old messages from fresh ones.

questions: how does ospf prevent replay attacks
what is the ospf boot count
why is the ip source address in the ospf hash
subtitle: How OSPFv2 manual keys get replay protection with a 64-bit sequence number and a hash that covers the sender's IP address.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication with manually configured keys can be fooled by replayed packets, within a session or across sessions, and it does not protect the IP source address.
tldr.mechanism: The sequence number grows to 64 bits (a boot count plus a 32-bit packet counter) and moves after the packet, the IP source address is mixed into the Apad constant, and a protocol ID is appended to the key.
tldr.outcome: Replayed or spoofed packets fail authentication and are dropped. The cost is that a router must keep its boot count in non-volatile storage.

facts.label: Apad constant
facts.value: 0x878FE1F3, first 4 octets set to the IP source address

today: RFC 7474 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5709, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Replay and Spoofing Problem
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication in RFC 2328 uses per-packet sequence numbers to resist replay attacks. The numbers are kept as part of neighbor adjacency state, so when an adjacency goes down the sequence numbers are reinitialized. The old mechanism also does not say what to do when a sequence number wraps. Attackers can exploit both gaps.

A second weakness is that the authentication in RFC 2328, as updated by RFC 5709, does not cover the IP header. On broadcast and NBMA networks OSPF identifies a neighbor by the IP source address, so changing that address can cause denial of service. Hello packets may be reflected so a neighbor appears to have one-way communication, and Database Description packets may be reflected to disrupt an adjacency.

This document changes the cryptographic authentication of RFC 5709 to close these holes. It updates RFC 2328 and RFC 5709, and it only covers manual key management.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky can record a real message and play it back later, or pretend to be a different sender. The old rules did not stop either trick very well.

sections.title: Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
The OSPFv2 sequence number grows to 64 bits. The low 32 bits hold a strictly increasing packet counter and the high 32 bits hold a boot count. Routers are required to keep the boot count in non-volatile storage for the deployed life of the router. The SNMPv3 snmpEngineBoots variable MAY be used, but a separate OSPF boot count is RECOMMENDED because it decouples SNMP reinitialization from OSPF reinitialization.

The low-order number MUST be incremented for every OSPF packet sent. On reception, the number MUST be greater than that of the last packet of the same type accepted from that neighbor. Otherwise the packet is treated as a replay and dropped. Packet types are tracked separately because prioritized packets can arrive out of order. If the 32-bit counter ever wraps, the boot count can be incremented to keep the combined number increasing.
sections.eli5: Each note carries a big number made of two parts: how many times the sender has restarted, and a counter that goes up with each note. A note with a number that is too small is old, so you ignore it.

sections.title: The New Authentication Type 3 Packet Layout
sections.content:
Authentication types 0, 1 and 2 already exist in RFC 2328. This document defines type 3. In the 64-bit authentication field of the OSPF header, the sequence number is removed, and the Key ID is extended to 32 bits and moved to the sequence number's old position. The zero field at the start of the authentication area grows from 16 bits to 24 bits.

There is no room in the header for a 64-bit number, so it is placed in the 8 octets right after the OSPF packet and is covered by the authentication digest. Those 8 octets are counted in the IP header length and the authentication data length, but not in the OSPF packet length.
sections.eli5: The number does not fit in the old spot on the envelope, so it is put on a tag right after the letter, and the secret code covers that tag too.

sections.title: Choosing Keys
sections.content:
Keys come from a key table, as in RFC 7210. A usable key must be valid for the current time (the send or accept lifetime, depending on direction) and for the chosen algorithm.

For unicast transmission the key's Peers field holds the area ID, or all if no key names the area. The Direction field must be out or both, and the Interfaces field must match the sending interface or be all. An explicit interface match is preferred over all, and ties go to the key with the most recent SendLifetimeStart, which makes key rollover graceful. Virtual links identify the far end by the transit area ID, a colon and the router ID. Multicast transmission uses the same ideas.

On reception the receiver uses the Key ID from the header to find the key. OSPFv2 keys are symmetric, so the local and peer key names are identical. The Direction must be in or both.
sections.eli5: A router keeps a keyring. It picks the key that is still valid, meant for the right neighbor and direction, and the newest one if several fit. The note says which key was used so the receiver can find the same one.

sections.title: Protecting the IP Source Address and Keys
sections.content:
The hash input now includes the 64-bit sequence number along with the OSPF packet and the authentication trailer. The trailer is filled with Apad, a constant of 0x878FE1F3 repeated. This document makes the first 4 octets of Apad equal to the IP source address, and the rest repeats 0x878FE1F3 (L - 4)/4 times, where L is the hash length in octets. Receivers MUST do the same with the source address of the incoming packet. If a rogue router changes the source address of a replayed packet, the hash no longer matches and the packet is dropped.

To stop cross-protocol replay between protocols that share keys, the two-octet OSPFv2 Cryptographic Protocol ID is appended to the key before use. The document also settles a detail left open: when Ko is XORed with Ipad or Opad, Ko MUST be padded with zeros to the pad length. Nothing else in the RFC 5709 process changes.
sections.eli5: The sender's address is stirred into the secret code. If someone changes the address on the envelope, the code stops matching and the note is thrown out.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The extension uses a new authentication type, so it needs no special transition rules. If a packet arrives whose AuType does not match the type configured on the interface, it is dropped as RFC 2328 already specifies. A mismatch with this type therefore behaves like any other authentication type mismatch.
sections.eli5: If a note comes in a style the receiver is not expecting, the receiver just ignores it, the same as it already does for any other style mismatch.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
This work covers only manual key management, as part of Phase 1 of the KARP working group. The document names two drawbacks. First, the boot count must survive in non-volatile storage. If that storage is repaired, upgraded or lost, or the router is replaced, the authentication keys MUST be changed to prevent replay. Second, a router taken out of service could in theory have its adjacency re-established by replaying a whole session, though the text calls this extremely unlikely. Replayed hellos alone would only cause superfluous processing, and changing the manual keys also defeats it.

A single sequence number can leave a router open to replay when the same source IP address is used on two point-to-point unnumbered links. Where an attacker can tap those links, use different keys on each.
sections.eli5: The router must remember how many times it has restarted, even if it loses power. If it forgets, you should change the secret keys so old notes cannot be replayed.
